title: Purpose
instruction: Learn what Oath & Action does, and how its pillars and nonpartisan rules shape every piece.
intro: Oath & Action is a nonpartisan publication and a set of tools for people in every state who live under public rules they rarely get to read. Our mission is “Help people understand and improve the rules that shape their lives.”

The ampersand in our name is the hinge, the joint a door swings on. It joins a promise to the action that keeps it, so every piece explains and tracks a decision, then turns to the people who make it and the step a reader can take. Chapter 04 draws the hinge and sets its rules.

groups.title: Color and party
groups.line: Give no party, side or person a color of its own, and print every name on its mark.

groups.title: Pictures
groups.line: Show real places and people doing public work, with a caption a reader can check.

groups.title: Choosing examples
groups.line: Spread examples across subjects, states, regions and levels of government, and log each one so anyone can count them.

groups.title: Words
groups.line: Name the office that decides, and describe every rule in words its supporters would accept.

groups.title: Hinge headlines
groups.line: Keep both halves equal and join people only through something they share; Rule 02.27 sets how to write a hinge headline and Rule 04.3 how to draw one.

groups.title: Labels, Act pieces and names
groups.line: Tell a reader what kind of piece they are reading, and name each product for what it does.

rules.title: Keep red off every party, side and person.
rule: Pillar Red never stands for a party, one side of a debate or a named person, in a chart, a map, a label or a headline. Each view gives its one working red to the job Rule 05.3 names, and none of those jobs is a side.

text: Election-night maps have taught readers to see red as one party. A red mark on a side tells a reader on the other side that the piece is against them before they read a word, and they stop trusting the record we keep for everyone.

correct.caption: Both sides of the vote take the same Charcoal, with their names and counts printed. The view’s one working red goes to the step a reader can take now, the button that follows the bill.

failure.caption: Red on the no votes casts those three senators as the problem. A reader who agrees with them sees an attack, and the count stops reading as a record.

specs.label: Working red
specs.value: One job per view, in the order Rule 05.3 sets

specs.label: Sides of a vote
specs.value: One neutral ink, names and counts printed

rules.builders: Search the piece for Pillar Red and name each red mark’s job. If a mark stands for a party, a side or a person, redraw it in the party mark ink with its name printed.

rules.title: Draw every party in one neutral ink, with its name on the mark.
rule: When a chart, map or table shows parties, draw every party’s mark in the same neutral ink, Charcoal on Newsprint, and print the party’s name on or beside its mark. Where two sides must be told apart at a glance, draw one solid and one in outline, in that same ink. Red never stands against blue or Verdigris.

text: Red against blue reads as an election before it reads as data, and red against Verdigris stages the same contest in other hues. One ink gives every party the same weight, and a printed name lets a reader see who is who without learning a color code, in color or in grayscale.

correct.caption: Both parties take the same Charcoal, with each party’s name beside its bar, so a finding of agreement reads as agreement.

failure.caption: Red and blue turn a finding of agreement into a contest, and the color key makes a reader match swatches to find each party, which fails in grayscale.

specs.label: Party marks
specs.value: Charcoal, one ink for every party

specs.label: Two sides at a glance
specs.value: One solid and one in outline, in the same ink

specs.label: Names
specs.value: Printed on or beside each mark, in the text ink

specs.label: Order
specs.value: Alphabetical, unless the data sets another order

rules.builders: Use the party mark token for every party, never a palette color by name, and set each party’s name as a direct label.

rules.title: Run a two-way scale from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris.
rule: A scale that shows change in two directions runs from Prussian through Newsprint to Verdigris. A boxed arrow and a word name each step’s direction, because the two hues lose their order in grayscale. Red and blue never form a two-way pair.

text: Neither end of the pair belongs to a party, so a fall and a rise carry the same weight. The arrow and the word carry the direction for a reader who sees no color at all.

correct.caption: Each step carries a boxed arrow and a word, so the key reads the same in grayscale.

failure.caption: A red-to-blue scale reads as one party’s gain against the other’s, whatever it measures, and with no arrows its direction disappears in grayscale.

specs.label: Steps
specs.value: Five, step 1 the strongest fall, step 3 the page color

specs.label: Direction
specs.value: A boxed arrow in each step’s label ink, and a word

rules.builders: Use the five diverging steps in order and draw each arrow in the matching diverging label token, which the chart palette pairs with its fill.

rules.title: On Prussian, turn identity marks White and data marks Newsprint.
rule: On a Prussian ground, set every identity mark in one color, White, the ampersand included. Draw data graphics on Prussian in Newsprint. Red never sits on Prussian.

text: Pillar Red measures 3.19 to 1 against Prussian, which passes the 3 to 1 WCAG asks of marks until the size drops. At 16 px, where smoothing thins the strokes, the red ampersand measures 2.27 to 1 and a White one 8.27 to 1. Red on our dark blue also pairs the two colors election maps give the parties.
why.basis: Design judgment, measured against WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 at rendered sizes

correct.caption: The wordmark and its ampersand turn White, and the bar turns Newsprint. The panel carries no red.

failure.caption: The red ampersand sinks into the Prussian ground at 3.19 to 1, and at small sizes a reader loses the mark’s center.

specs.label: Identity marks
specs.value: White, one color

specs.label: Data marks
specs.value: Newsprint

rules.builders: Inside a Prussian surface class, the identity signature token resolves to White and the data emphasis token to Newsprint. Never name the palette red there.

rules.title: Color a map by the rule or measure the story covers.
rule: Color a map by the rule, count or measure the story is about, never by which party won each place. Use the neutral palette or a pattern, and set the key beside the map.

text: A map colored by winner splits the country into two camps and gives large, thinly settled states the most ink. What a reader wants to know is whether a rule reaches the place where they live.

correct.caption: Solid, hatched and open tiles show the rule, with the key next to the map and the source below it.

failure.caption: Colored by winner, the map splits the country into two camps and says nothing about the rule a story covers.

specs.label: Tile grid
specs.value: 12 columns by 8 rows, one square per state and DC

specs.label: Fills
specs.value: Charcoal, a Charcoal hatch and open, keyed in words

rules.builders: Start from our shared tile grid and join the story’s own measure to it by state code. A map of election results follows chapter 14’s rules, with party names printed.

rules.title: Show domes, columns and flags only in a captioned photograph of that place.
rule: Show a capitol dome, columns or a flag only inside a documentary photograph of that place or event, with a caption that names it. Keep them out of icons, backgrounds and textures.

text: Campaigns in both parties use the dome and the flag as shorthand for government. As decoration they stand for no rule, office or event, so they give the reader nothing to check or act on.

correct.caption: The building appears only as the place where the vote happened, named in a caption, in a photograph still to be made.

failure.caption: The dome behind the headline decorates a story about one vote and borrows the look of campaign mail, and the card names no office.

rules.builders: Build cards from type and the brand’s own devices. A dome, a column or a flag enters only with a documentary photograph, its caption and its credit.

rules.title: Keep party symbols, candidate photos, campaign gear and protest slogans out of brand graphics.
rule: Keep party symbols, candidate photographs, campaign merchandise and legible protest slogans out of brand graphics, since each takes a side the piece never argued. A party’s logo may appear as evidence, inside a sourced document the piece reproduces.

text: A reader takes any symbol on our page as ours. A campaign button or a slogan placard reads as an endorsement, even when the story beside it is neutral.

correct.caption: The card explains both votes and points to the ballot text as its document.

failure.caption: The button and the placard take sides on a measure the card set out to explain, so a reader on either side stops at the picture.

rules.builders: When a story needs a party’s logo or a campaign’s material, place the whole document as a sourced image with its credit, never the symbol by itself.

rules.title: Photograph people doing public work, and caption who, what, where and when.
rule: Choose photographs of people of different ages, places and roles doing public work, officials among them. Every caption names who is shown, what they are doing, where and when.

text: A reader trusts a picture of a real hearing more than a picture of the idea of one, and a full caption lets them check it.

correct.caption: The caption names the person by role, the act, the place and the time.

failure.caption: The caption names no person, act, place or date, so a reader cannot check the picture and learns nothing from it.

rules.builders: Write the caption’s four parts before a photograph goes in: who, what, where and when.

rules.title: Draw no more than one example in four from one atlas domain, or one in five from one state.
rule: Count examples within one unit: a chapter of this guide, a report, or a month of newsletter issues. Draw no more than one in four from any one of our systems atlas’s ten domains, and no more than one in five from any one state.

text: A run of examples from one subject or one state tells readers whose problems we care about. Rotation keeps a reader in Texas and a reader in Maine in view of the same chapter.

correct.caption: This chapter checked against its own rule: no domain supplies more than three of its 15 examples, under one in four, and no named state supplies more than one.

failure.caption: Three election examples from one state would tell readers elsewhere that the chapter was written for someone else.

rules.builders: Count from the rotation log before a chapter, report or month of issues runs, using the atlas’s ten domains by their full names.

rules.title: Rotate examples across levels of government and regions.
rule: Draw examples from federal, state, county or city, and school district decisions, and from every region of the country: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South and the West.

text: Most of the rules that reach a household are written below the federal level. A reader who only ever sees Congress learns that the decisions nearest to them are not worth following.

correct.caption: This chapter’s examples reach all four levels, and its real cases come from all four regions: Texas in the South, California in the West, Ohio in the Midwest and Pennsylvania in the Northeast.

failure.caption: Four federal examples in a row leave out the councils, boards and districts where a reader can most easily be heard.

rules.builders: Tag each row of the rotation log with its level and region, and look for an empty one before the piece runs.

rules.title: When majorities of both parties use a mechanism, show a case from each.
rule: When majorities of both parties use the same mechanism, show a documented case from each, described in the same form and at the same length. The test case is Loop R4a, the map-drawing loop, which our systems atlas titles “Majorities draw maps that help them keep control.”

text: A mechanism shown through one party’s case reads as a charge against that party. With a case from each side, told the same way, the mechanism itself stands out, and that is the part a reader can change.

correct.caption: Each case names the month, the majority that acted, the seats its map aimed at and the step that put the map in place, in 23 words.

failure.caption: With one party’s case alone, the loop reads as a charge against that party, and a reader who votes for it stops at the first line.

rules.builders: Before a piece runs a mechanism, list the party of the majority in each of the atlas’s case records for that loop, pick one case from each and write both in the same form.

rules.title: Log each example’s domain, state, region, level and backing coalition.
rule: Log every example with its atlas domain, its state and region, its level of government and, for any reform shown, the coalition that usually backs it. Our editors review the log before each chapter, report or series runs.

text: A chapter can lean toward one topic or one side without anyone noticing. A log turns balance into counts anyone can check, including a reader who suspects a lean.

correct.caption: Every field is filled, and an invented example says so in the state, region and coalition columns.

failure.caption: A row with blank fields cannot be counted, so whoever checks the log cannot see a run of one topic or one side’s reforms.

rules.builders: Keep one log row per example in the piece’s notes and count domains, states and regions from it before it runs.

rules.title: Name the office that decides, and name a party only when party is the mechanism.
rule: Say which office or body makes the decision. Name a party only when party is part of how the decision works, such as a party-line vote, and give the count and its source.

text: A reader can call an office or testify before it, and at the next election they can vote out its members or the official who appointed them. A party’s name in place of an office gives them a team to blame and nobody to call.

correct.caption: The sentence names the commission and the hearing where it decides, so a reader knows where to look.

failure.caption: “Politicians” names no office, so the reader has no one to call, and “again” supplies a grievance the record does not show.

rules.builders: Search a draft for “politicians”, “Washington”, “lawmakers” and party names, and replace each with the office that holds the decision.

rules.title: Ask questions a supporter of the current rule could ask too.
rule: Leave grievance words out of headlines, questions and calls to act, such as “rigged”, “broken”, “crisis” and “the rule you are angry about”. Write each question so a person who supports the current rule could ask it too.

text: A question that assumes the reader is angry tells half our readers the piece is for someone else. Who decided, and when the rule could change, are things a reader on either side of it wants to know.

correct.caption: A homeowner who likes today’s rate and one who wants it lower would both click this question.

failure.caption: The question assumes the reader is angry and that someone wronged them, so a reader who likes the rule has no reason to read on.

rules.builders: Search a draft for the words this rule lists, and read each question as someone who likes the current rule would.

rules.title: Use plain verbs in place of war and sports metaphors.
rule: Describe a public decision in the words for what happens, such as propose, debate, vote and pass. Leave out war and sports metaphors such as fight, battle, front and game plan.

text: A war or a game needs an enemy or a loser, and the people on the other side of a vote are our readers too. The verbs for what happens also tell a reader where the decision stands.

correct.caption: The series name is Dispatch, and the headline names the vote and its day. Only the headline is invented, so the label sits beside it.

failure.caption: “From the Front”, our fifth edition’s series name, and “battle” cast the vote as a war with an enemy, and the headline never says when the vote happens.

rules.builders: Search a draft for fight, battle, front, war and game plan, and name the step in the process in its place.

rules.title: Show both readings of a contested claim at the same length.
rule: When credible studies disagree, give the two readings equal length, the same verbs and the same type, and name who holds each one in the same form.

text: Equal space is how a reader sees that the disagreement is real. A long reading beside a short dismissal, or a credential on one side and a tag on the other, tells them which side we prefer before they weigh either.

correct.caption: Each reading runs 24 words, uses the verb “find” and names who holds it the same way, by role and by the organization they wrote for.

failure.caption: One reading becomes “the research” and the other three small words, so the layout settles a question the evidence leaves open.

rules.builders: Set both readings in one two-column block with matching labels, describe both holders in the same words, and count the words of each before you publish.

rules.title: Describe a rule so its supporters would accept the description.
rule: Read your description of a rule as someone who supports it would. If they would object to the words, rewrite the description until they would accept it, and save the argument for a labeled position piece.

text: Readers who back a rule are among the people we serve, and many are the officials we ask readers to contact, so the description has to hold for them as well.

correct.caption: A senator who values the 60-vote rule and one who wants it gone would both sign off on this sentence about the same rule.

failure.caption: “Hold the country hostage” is an opponent’s charge, so a senator who values the rule would reject the sentence before reaching the facts.

rules.builders: Before the piece runs, read the description in the place of someone who supports the rule, and mark every word they would change.

rules.title: Set both halves of a hinge headline in one color and weight, and give the red to the ampersand.
rule: Set both noun phrases of a hinge headline in the same ink, face and weight. The ampersand takes the view’s working red, unless an error or a step on the same view already holds it; then the ampersand takes the headline’s ink, as Rule 04.3 sets out.

text: When one half is red or heavier, the headline takes a side between a rule and its result. Equal halves leave the joining to the ampersand.

correct.caption: Both halves share Charcoal and ExtraBold, and ampersand B carries the red.

failure.caption: The red second half reads as the alarm and the first half as its cause, and the ampersand no longer stands out as the join.

rules.builders: Set the headline in Inter Tight ExtraBold and place ampersand B at the cap height in place of the font’s ampersand, from the master Rule 04.3 names for the size.

rules.title: Join people through a rule or place they share, and rotate their order.
rule: When a hinge headline joins two people or groups, join them through a rule or a place they share. Swap their order from one piece to the next, so neither always comes first.

text: The ampersand stands for common ground, and people stand on it through something they share. A fixed order would rank one group above the other.

correct.caption: The rider and the driver share a route, then a hearing, and the next piece puts the driver first.

failure.caption: “Us” and “them” name two sides with nothing shared between them, so the ampersand marks a divide.

rules.builders: Log the order of each pair of people, and swap it the next time a piece joins the same two groups.

rules.title: Name parties, the left or the right in a hinge headline only to report sourced agreement.
rule: Use “left”, “right” or a party’s name in a hinge headline only to report a point where the sides agree, such as a bill with sponsors from both parties. Join the two through what they agree on, as Rule 01.19 asks of every pair of people, and source the agreement in the deck.

text: A red ampersand between two sides would mark the sides themselves, against Rule 01.1. Reporting agreement is the one case where naming the sides helps a reader.

correct.caption: The headline joins both parties’ voters through the ban they agree on, and the deck gives the figures and their source.

failure.caption: The red ampersand sits between two sides with no shared fact, so it marks the divide and reports nothing.

rules.builders: When a headline names the sides, link the deck’s source line to the vote, the sponsor list or the survey that shows the agreement.

rules.title: Open every kicker with one content label.
rule: Open the kicker, the short line above a headline, with one of the seven content labels in this rule’s specifications. At most one more part follows, after a middle dot: the series name if the piece belongs to a series, otherwise its topic, as in “Explainer · Local schools”. A newsletter issue carries no label in its header, and each story inside it carries its own.

text: The label tells a reader what kind of claim the piece makes before they read it, and whether we are reporting or arguing.

correct.caption: Each kicker opens with its label and adds at most a series or a topic. Only “Our position” takes the Charcoal fill. The first three headlines are real, so the label sits beside each invented one.

failure.caption: “Explain” is a pillar and says nothing about the claim. “Must read” and “Breaking” push the reader and hide that the piece argues, and the third kicker reaches its label only after the series.

specs.label: Explainer
specs.value: How a rule or a decision works

specs.label: Tracker
specs.value: Where a decision stands, dated “as of”

specs.label: Analysis
specs.value: What the evidence shows on a contested question

specs.label: Report
specs.value: A numbered study, with its method and its date

specs.label: Guide
specs.value: How to reach the office that decides, for a Connect piece

specs.label: Act · How to take part
specs.value: One step with its date and place; one label, with nothing after it

specs.label: Our position
specs.value: An argument for or against a named measure, in the Charcoal label (Rule 01.23)

specs.label: Never a kicker
specs.value: A pillar name alone, and a chart’s “Finding” line, which sits above the chart’s title as its evidence line

specs.label: Type
specs.value: The label style, Inter 700 capitals at 13 px; the second part in the secondary text ink

rules.builders: Pick the label from the seven in this rule. If a piece fits none of them, ask the editor before it runs. Rule 08.8 sets the grid and icon that may lead a kicker.

rules.title: In a process piece, name the step and leave the side to the reader.
rule: An Act piece labeled “Act · How to take part” gives one step with its date and place, sets out what supporters and opponents have said at the same length, and takes no side. Its ask is the view’s one working red.

text: A reader of any view can use a process piece, because it tells them how to be heard and leaves what to say to them.

correct.caption: The piece names who decides, gives both sides one sentence each, then turns at the hinge divider to two dated ways to take part. The red sits on the ask alone.

failure.caption: The piece keeps the process label and then argues one side, so a reader who opposes the change meets a position they were told was not there.

specs.label: Kicker
specs.value: Act · How to take part, the label alone

specs.label: Ask
specs.value: Pillar Red fill, White label at 19 px bold, Charcoal keyline on Newsprint

specs.label: Before the ask
specs.value: The hinge divider, its ampersand in the surface’s ink

specs.label: Width
specs.value: Shown as a phone page, 360 px wide, with the phone sizes of the type scale; on a wider screen the column grows to the reading measure

rules.builders: Build the ending from the hinge divider, the “What you can do” line and one ask button. Link the neutral tracker, never a campaign page.

rules.title: Put a position piece’s label before the headline and its fairness kit before the ask.
rule: A piece that asks readers to support or oppose a named measure opens its kicker with the label “Our position”, before the headline. Before the ask it carries the fairness kit, the eight parts in this rule’s specifications, among them the strongest case against the position, what we don’t know and who decided.

text: A reader who disagrees with us can still trust the rest of our coverage when each argument carries its label, its strongest opposing case and the names of the people who decided it.

correct.caption: The label comes first, the case against comes before the ask, and the disclosure of who decided, when and with what funder interest sits directly above the button.

failure.caption: With the label at the bottom and no case against, a reader learns the piece was an argument only after the ask, which reads as a trick.

specs.label: Label first
specs.value: “Our position” opens the kicker, before the headline, and a shared card keeps it top left.

specs.label: The strongest case against
specs.value: The opposing case as its supporters would put it, sourced, at least a third of the argument’s length.

specs.label: Grades kept
specs.value: Every claim keeps its evidence grade, and its verb matches the grade.

specs.label: Opponents by role
specs.value: Name opponents by office or role, and cast no party as a villain.

specs.label: What we don’t know
specs.value: The open questions, named.

specs.label: Process facts
specs.value: Who decides, when and how, word for word as the neutral tracker gives them.

specs.label: Disclosure
specs.value: Who decided the position and when, any funder’s interest in the measure, and links to the bios of those who decided, above the ask.

specs.label: Kept out of the record
specs.value: Positions stay out of the atlas, the trackers and the data.

rules.builders: Use the position label component, never a plain kicker, and check the eight parts of the kit in this rule’s specifications before the piece goes to the editor.

rules.title: Name each product for what it does, and keep the ampersand for Oath & Action.
rule: Give each product a plain name that says what it does, signed by Oath & Action. The atlas is the only product named as a question, and no product name holds an ampersand. When we type a partner’s name in our own copy, its ampersand becomes “and”, and the partner’s logo stays as the partner draws it.

text: Every product carries one name, Oath & Action, so a reader who trusts the newsletter can trust the tracker it links to. A plain name tells them what they will get before they open it.

correct.caption: Each name says what the product does, and the only ampersand belongs to Oath & Action.

failure.caption: A second ampersand competes with ours, a scorecard grades the officials we ask readers to contact, and “the Front” turns a series into a war.

rules.builders: Name a new product as its subject plus its kind, such as “Child Care Rules Tracker”, and check the name against this rule and Rule 01.15 before it ships. A piece made with a partner goes to Dustin Cathcart, our founder and editor, or an editor he names, before it prints or posts, and the host’s name leads. Chapter 03 sets the partnership lockup.

extras.label: Words this guide uses
extras.caption: Each word is defined once here and kept the same through the guide. The link beside it opens the rule or chapter that sets it.

extras.label: The hinge in the locked lines
extras.caption: Each locked line splits at the hinge, a commitment first and the action after it. The pillars split the same way, between Track and Connect, where a reader stops learning about a decision and starts taking part in it.

extras.label: The four pillars, always in this order
extras.caption: Every product carries the Oath & Action name. The atlas, the trackers and the data never take a position; positions appear only in labeled Act pieces. Chapter 09 draws the pillar marks.

extras.label: One piece from each pillar, at true size
extras.caption: Each piece is 340 px wide, the text column of a phone, and opens with its kicker, turns at the hinge divider to “What you can do” and ends on one step, the view’s one working red. Explain and Track quote real records. Connect and Act are invented, and each carries the Illustrative label at its head.

extras.label: Our founding line
extras.caption: Chapter 02’s table of brand lines lists it with no role.
